nodes.title: Logic & Quantifiers
objectives: Master propositional logic, truth tables, and equivalences
Express mathematical claims rigorously using universal and existential quantifiers
Negate complex quantified statements without logical leakage
nodes.primer: Logic is the operating system of formal mathematics. Before proving theorems, we must establish the syntax of truth: propositions, implications, and quantifiers (∀, ∃). A statement P => Q is false strictly when P is true and Q is false.

resources.title: Book of Proof - Chapter 2: Logic
resources.description: Open textbook treatment of logical statements and quantifiers.

hooks: Why is (P => Q) logically equivalent to (¬P ∨ Q) in microprocessor circuit design?

nodes.title: Proof Techniques
objectives: Execute direct proofs, contrapositive, and contradiction
Construct mathematical induction proofs with robust base cases
nodes.primer: A mathematical proof is an irrefutable deduction from axioms. Contrapositive leverages the equivalence (P => Q) <=> (¬Q => ¬P). Contradiction assumes ¬P and derives a falsehood. Induction establishes a domino chain across the natural numbers.

resources.title: MIT OCW 6.042J: Mathematics for Computer Science - Proofs
resources.description: Standard rigorous introduction to proof methods.

hooks: How does mathematical induction guarantee loop invariants in verified software?

nodes.title: Vectors & Matrices
objectives: Understand vectors as geometric displacements and algebraic tuples
Perform matrix multiplication as composition of linear transformations
nodes.primer: Matrices are not mere spreadsheets of numbers; they are active geometric operators that stretch, rotate, and sheer space. Matrix multiplication AB represents applying transformation B followed by transformation A.

resources.title: 3Blue1Brown - Essence of Linear Algebra
resources.description: The gold standard visual intuition for linear transformations.

hooks: How do 3D graphics engines transform millions of vertices in nanoseconds?

nodes.title: Linear Systems & Gaussian Elimination
objectives: Solve linear systems using row operations and echelon forms
Characterize existence and uniqueness of solutions via pivot columns
nodes.primer: A system Ax = b asks: which linear combination of the columns of A produces vector b? Gaussian elimination systematically reduces [A|b] to row echelon form using elementary row operations without altering the solution space.

resources.title: Gilbert Strang - MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra Lecture 2
resources.description: Classic lecture on elimination with matrices.

hooks: Why does computing robot arm joint equilibrium reduce to solving Ax = b?

nodes.title: Linear Maps, Rank & Nullspace
objectives: Compute the nullspace (kernel) and column space (image) of a matrix
State and apply the Rank-Nullity Theorem: rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(V)
nodes.primer: A linear transformation T: V -> W preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication. The nullspace contains all inputs collapsed to zero; the column space contains all possible outputs. The Rank-Nullity theorem guarantees that dimension is conserved.

resources.title: Linear Algebra Done Right - Axler Chapter 3
resources.description: Coordinate-free conceptual perspective on linear maps.

hooks: When a robotic arm loses a degree of freedom (singularity), which subspace gains dimension?

nodes.title: Determinants
objectives: Compute determinants via cofactor expansion and row operations
Interpret det(A) geometrically as signed volume scaling factor
nodes.primer: The determinant det(A) measures how much a transformation scales volume. In 2D, it is the signed area of the unit square after transformation; in 3D, signed volume. A determinant of zero means space has collapsed to a lower dimension, making the matrix non-invertible.

resources.title: 3Blue1Brown - The Determinant
resources.description: Visual exploration of volume scaling.

hooks: Why does the change-of-variables formula in multivariable calculus require the Jacobian determinant?

nodes.title: Eigenvalues & Diagonalisation
objectives: Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors via the characteristic equation det(A - λI) = 0
Interpret eigenvectors geometrically as invariant directions
Diagonalise matrices A = PDP^-1 to compute high matrix powers A^k
nodes.primer: Most vectors change direction when multiplied by a matrix A. Eigenvectors are the privileged directions that only get stretched by a factor λ: Av = λv. In the eigenvector basis, the transformation is purely diagonal, decoupling complex coupled systems.

resources.title: Gilbert Strang - MIT 18.06 Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
resources.description: Intuitive foundation of eigenvectors.

hooks: Why do Google PageRank and the resonant frequencies of bridges both depend on eigenvalues?

nodes.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) & PCA
objectives: Decompose any matrix into A = U Σ V^T
Apply SVD to low-rank approximation and Principal Component Analysis
nodes.primer: While diagonalisation requires square matrices and independent eigenvectors, SVD works on any rectangular matrix. It identifies orthonormal bases for the domain and codomain such that the matrix acts purely as coordinate stretching along principal axes.

resources.title: Steve Brunton - Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
resources.description: Clear data-driven applied view of SVD and dimensionality reduction.

hooks: How do computer vision models compress high-dimensional facial images into 50 eigenfaces?

nodes.title: Programming Fundamentals (Python)
objectives: Master control flow, functions, recursion, and core data types
Write idiomatic, modular, and cleanly tested Python functions
nodes.primer: Programming is the precise expression of algorithmic thought. In Python, functions are first-class citizens, duck-typing allows flexibility, and concise idioms (list comprehensions, generators) express complex transformations with high clarity.

resources.title: Python Official Tutorial
resources.description: Official guide to Python syntax and structures.

hooks: How does Python handle memory references under the hood?

nodes.title: Data Structures (Arrays, Linked Lists, Hash Maps, Trees)
objectives: Implement arrays, linked lists, hash tables, heaps, and binary search trees
Analyze memory layout and cache locality trade-offs
nodes.primer: Data structures organize information to enable efficient algorithmic operations. Contiguous memory (arrays) optimizes cache hits, while pointer-based structures (trees, graphs) provide dynamic flexibility at the expense of memory overhead.

resources.title: CS50 - Data Structures
resources.description: Foundational visual understanding of memory allocation and pointer data structures.

hooks: Why is traversing a contiguous array up to 50x faster than a linked list due to CPU L1 cache lines?

nodes.title: Complexity Analysis (Big-O, Recurrences)
objectives: Derive asymptotic time and space bounds using Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta
Solve divide-and-conquer recurrence relations via the Master Theorem
nodes.primer: Asymptotic complexity evaluates how resource usage scales as problem size n grows toward infinity. It abstracts hardware variance to reveal fundamental mathematical efficiency barriers.

resources.title: MIT 6.006 - Introduction to Algorithms
resources.description: Formal asymptotic notation and recurrence analysis.

hooks: Why can an O(n log n) algorithm process a trillion items in hours while an O(n^2) algorithm takes 30,000 years?

nodes.title: Graph Algorithms (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, A*)
objectives: Traverse graphs using BFS (queue) and DFS (stack/recursion)
Find shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm and heuristic A* search
nodes.primer: Graphs model relational topology. BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs by expanding uniform concentric frontiers. Dijkstra generalizes this using a priority queue for positive edge weights. A* injects an admissible heuristic h(n) to direct exploration toward the goal.

resources.title: Red Blob Games - Introduction to A*
resources.description: The definitive interactive visual guide to pathfinding.

hooks: How does an autonomous mobile robot plan obstacle-free routes in a factory within milliseconds?

nodes.title: Dynamic Programming
objectives: Identify optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
Formulate Bellman equations and implement memoization / tabulation
nodes.primer: Dynamic programming trades space for time by caching solutions to overlapping subproblems. If a global optimum is composed of optimal solutions to subproblems, the problem can be broken down recursively into a DAG of state transitions.

resources.title: MIT 6.006 - Dynamic Programming
resources.description: Systematic 5-step framework for DP.

hooks: How does dynamic programming power both biological sequence alignment and robot trajectory optimization?

nodes.title: Rigid-Body Transforms (SO(3), SE(3))
objectives: Represent 3D rotations via rotation matrices, Euler angles, and unit quaternions
Compose homogeneous transformation matrices in SE(3) to relate reference frames
nodes.primer: Robotics is the science of spatial coordinate transformations. A rigid body has 6 degrees of freedom (3 position, 3 orientation). Homogeneous 4x4 transformation matrices in SE(3) combine rotation and translation into a single unified matrix multiplication.

resources.title: Modern Robotics - Lynch & Park, Chapter 3
resources.description: The definitive textbook on screw theory and modern robot kinematics.

hooks: Why do spacecraft and drones use quaternions instead of Euler angles to avoid gimbal lock?

nodes.title: Forward & Inverse Kinematics
objectives: Compute end-effector pose from joint angles (Forward Kinematics)
Solve the inverse problem: finding joint angles to achieve a desired Cartesian target
nodes.primer: Forward kinematics computes the hand position from the angles of all robot joints using geometric chains. Inverse kinematics reverses this: given a target point in 3D space, which angles must the motors turn to? It often has multiple solutions, singular configurations, or no physical solution.

resources.title: Modern Robotics Chapter 4 & 6
resources.description: Kinematic chains and numerical inverse kinematics.

hooks: How does an insect or robot leg calculate joint bends to place its foot precisely on uneven rock?

nodes.title: Feedback Control (PID to State-Space)
objectives: Tune proportional-integral-derivative (PID) feedback loops
Model dynamical systems in state-space form dx/dt = Ax + Bu
nodes.primer: Open-loop commands drift due to friction and disturbances. Feedback control continuously measures the error e(t) = target - actual and applies correction proportional to the current error (P), accumulated past error (I), and anticipated rate of change (D).

resources.title: Brian Douglas - Control Systems Lectures
resources.description: Intuitive explanations of transfer functions and PID tuning.

hooks: How does a self-balancing Segway or quadrotor stay upright despite wind gusts?

nodes.title: Insect Morphology & Body Plan
objectives: Identify tagmata: head, thorax (pro, meso, meta), and abdomen
Analyze exoskeleton biomechanics, chitin structure, and jointed appendages
nodes.primer: Insects are the most successful animal body plan on Earth. Their bodies are divided into three specialized tagmata: head (sensory/feeding), thorax (locomotor engine with 3 pairs of legs and 2 pairs of wings), and abdomen (visceral organs and reproduction), enclosed in a lightweight chitinous exoskeleton.

resources.title: Amateur Entomologists' Society - Insect Anatomy
resources.description: Detailed morphological diagrams of insect structures.

hooks: How do insect joint mechanisms inspire resilient micro-robot flexures?

nodes.title: Social Insects & Colony Organization
objectives: Understand eusociality criteria (cooperative brood care, overlapping generations, caste division)
Analyze stigmergy and chemical pheromone trail reinforcement
nodes.primer: An ant colony is a superorganism. With no central leader, thousands of simple agents solve NP-hard routing, climate control, and foraging logistics through local interactions and stigmergy—modifying the environment with pheromones to guide collective action.

resources.title: E.O. Wilson - The Insect Societies
resources.description: Foundational text on social insect organization.

hooks: How do ant colonies solve distributed shortest-path problems without any ant knowing the map?

nodes.title: Celestial Coordinate Systems & The Sky
objectives: Navigate the celestial sphere using Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec)
Translate between local horizon coordinates (Alt/Az) and equatorial coordinates
nodes.primer: To map the cosmos, we project the earth's coordinate grid onto the celestial sphere. Right ascension mirrors longitude (measured in hours, minutes, seconds), while declination mirrors latitude (degrees north/south of the celestial equator).

resources.title: Crash Course Astronomy - Naked Eye Observations
resources.description: Engaging visual introduction to celestial navigation.

hooks: How did ancient mariners and Apollo astronauts use stellar angles to locate themselves in the void?

nodes.title: Celestial Mechanics & Keplerian Orbits
objectives: State and apply Kepler's three laws of planetary motion
Calculate orbital elements: semimajor axis, eccentricity, period
nodes.primer: Planets orbit in ellipses with the Sun at one focus (1st law). Equal areas are swept in equal times, implying faster velocity at perihelion (2nd law). The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis (3rd law), derived from Newton's inverse-square gravity.

resources.title: NASA - Kepler's Laws
resources.description: Official orbital mechanics primer.

hooks: Why do interplanetary spacecraft follow curved Hohmann transfer ellipses rather than straight lines?

nodes.title: Historical Thinking & Source Criticism
objectives: Distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary sources
Evaluate provenance, audience, corroboration, and historical bias
nodes.primer: History is not a passive ledger of dates; it is a critical discipline of evidentiary reconstruction. Source criticism interrogates who wrote a document, why they wrote it, what assumptions they held, and how their testimony corroborates with material archaeology.

resources.title: Stanford History Education Group - Reading Like a Historian
resources.description: Core methods of primary source analysis.

hooks: How do historians detect deliberate omissions and state propaganda in ancient inscriptions?

nodes.title: History of Mathematics & Science
objectives: Trace the historical impetus behind the invention of calculus (Newton & Leibniz)
Understand the transition from geometric intuition to 19th-century rigor (Cauchy, Weierstrass)
nodes.primer: Mathematical concepts do not descend from the heavens fully formed; they are forged to solve pressing physical dilemmas. Calculus arose directly from 17th-century astronomy and ballistics: the need to compute instantaneous velocity and planetary tangents.

resources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive
resources.description: Extensive scholarly archive of mathematical development.

hooks: Why did Newton conceal his calculus discoveries in anagrams for over twenty years?

nodes.title: Sensation, Perception & Feature Detection
objectives: Examine sensory transduction and receptive fields in the visual cortex
Connect biological edge detection (Hubel & Wiesel) to convolutional filters
nodes.primer: Perception is not a passive photograph; it is an active inferential reconstruction. The visual system decomposes light into primal visual features—oriented edges, contrast gradients, and motion vectors—via receptive fields in area V1.

resources.title: Nobel Prize in Medicine 1981 - Hubel & Wiesel
resources.description: Seminal discovery of visual cortical architecture.

hooks: Why does a modern Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) learn the exact same Gabor edge filters found in human V1?

nodes.title: Learning, Memory & The Spacing Effect
objectives: Analyze the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, consolidation, and retrieval practice
Examine how spaced repetition algorithms (FSRS) model human memory stability
nodes.primer: Retrieval is a memory modifier: testing yourself on a concept strengthens its neural representation far more than passive re-reading. The spacing effect demonstrates that expanding intervals between retrievals forces durable synaptic consolidation.

resources.title: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning
resources.description: Summary of cognitive psychology research on deliberate retrieval.

hooks: Why does struggling to recall an answer right before you forget it produce 300% greater retention than studying while fresh?

bridges.title: Ant Foraging ↔ Graph Shortest Paths
bridges.insight: Ant colony foraging is a decentralized shortest-path algorithm. Through positive feedback (reinforcing successful pheromone trails) and evaporation (decaying obsolete routes), ants converge onto minimal paths without any global graph representation.

challenge.prompt: Sketch the pheromone update equation: τ_ij(t+1) = (1 - ρ)·τ_ij(t) + Σ Δτ_ij. Which parameter prevents ants from getting permanently stuck in suboptimal loops?
challenge.starterHint: Think about the role of the evaporation coefficient ρ.

bridges.explainPrompt: How does ant colony trail reinforcement mathematically mirror edge relaxation and heuristic search in graph algorithms?

bridges.title: Eigenvalues ↔ Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
bridges.insight: Finding the principal axes of maximum variance in high-dimensional data is identical to finding the eigenvectors of the empirical covariance matrix. The dominant eigenvalue tells you exactly how much statistical variance is preserved along that axis.

challenge.prompt: Given covariance matrix Σ = (1/n) X^T X, write the optimization problem that yields the first principal component as an eigenvalue equation.
challenge.starterHint: Maximize v^T Σ v subject to ||v||^2 = 1 using Lagrange multipliers.

bridges.explainPrompt: Why does the direction of greatest statistical variance correspond to the largest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix?

bridges.title: Eigenvalues ↔ Dynamic Stability in Robotics
bridges.insight: For a linear robot dynamical system dx/dt = Ax, the real parts of the eigenvalues of matrix A determine whether the system is stable, oscillatory, or catastrophically diverging. Negative real parts guarantee asymptotic decay back to equilibrium.

challenge.prompt: If a 2-joint arm controller has system matrix A with eigenvalues λ1 = -2 + 3i and λ2 = -2 - 3i, describe the resulting motion when perturbed from rest.
challenge.starterHint: Examine the real part (-2) vs the imaginary part (±3i).

bridges.explainPrompt: Why do negative real eigenvalues ensure that an autonomous robot returns safely to its setpoint after a physical bump?

bridges.title: Biological Receptive Fields ↔ Convolutional Filters
bridges.insight: Hubel and Wiesel discovered that neurons in primate visual cortex V1 fire only in response to oriented bars of light. Fifty years later, convolutional neural networks trained on natural images independently learn identical Gabor edge filters in their first layers.

challenge.prompt: Explain how a 3x3 Sobel edge filter approximates a directional spatial derivative in digital image processing.

bridges.explainPrompt: Why is local spatial feature extraction biologically and computationally superior to processing raw pixels or photons globally?

items.prompt: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) on an adjacency list representation of a graph with V vertices and E edges? Enter in standard Big-O notation like O(V + E).
items.solution: Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once (O(V)), and each edge incident to a vertex is scanned when exploring its adjacency list (O(E)), giving total time O(V + E).
hints: How many times does each vertex enter and leave the queue?
How many times are edges examined across all adjacency lists?
Sum the vertex operations and edge operations.
The asymptotic bound is linear in vertices plus edges.
O(V + E)

items.prompt: What is the logical negation of the statement: 'Every continuous function is differentiable'?

answerKey.value: There exists a continuous function that is not differentiable.

items.solution: The statement has the form ∀f (Cont(f) => Diff(f)). Its negation is ¬(∀f (Cont(f) => Diff(f))) ≡ ∃f ¬(Cont(f) => Diff(f)) ≡ ∃f (Cont(f) ∧ ¬Diff(f)). Thus, there exists at least one continuous function that is not differentiable (e.g. Weierstrass function, or f(x) = |x| at 0).
hints: Identify the quantifier: 'Every' is a universal quantifier (∀).
What is the dual of a universal quantifier under negation?
Negating ∀x P(x) yields ∃x ¬P(x).
What is the negation of P => Q?
The negation is: There exists a continuous function that is not differentiable.

items.prompt: If proposition P is False and proposition Q is False, evaluate the truth value of the implication P => Q. Enter True or False.
items.solution: In classical logic, P => Q is defined as ¬P ∨ Q. Since P is False, ¬P is True, so ¬P ∨ Q is True. An implication with a false antecedent is vacuously true.
hints: Look at the definition of implication: P => Q.
When is an implication P => Q false?
An implication is ONLY false when the hypothesis P is True and conclusion Q is False.
Since hypothesis P is False, what must the truth value be?
The truth value is True.

items.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Enter the values as a comma-separated list.
items.solution: The characteristic equation is det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)^2 - 1 = 0 \implies (2-\lambda) = \pm 1 \implies \lambda \in \{1, 3\}.
hints: What is the characteristic equation for any 2x2 matrix A?
Set det(A - λI) = 0 and expand the 2x2 determinant (a-λ)(d-λ) - bc.
Expand (2 - λ)(2 - λ) - 1*1 = 0 to get λ² - 4λ + 3 = 0.
Factor the quadratic λ² - 4λ + 3 into (λ - 1)(λ - 3) = 0.
The eigenvalues are λ = 1 and λ = 3.

items.prompt: Arrange the following steps in logical order to prove: 'If v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ, then v is an eigenvector of A² with eigenvalue λ²'.

steps.text: Start with the given eigenvector equation: A v = λ v.
Multiply both sides on the left by matrix A: A(A v) = A(λ v).
Apply associativity on the left and scalar linearity on the right: A² v = λ(A v).
Substitute the identity A v = λ v into the right side: A² v = λ(λ v) = λ² v.
Conclude that A² v = λ² v with v ≠ 0, so v is an eigenvector of A² with eigenvalue λ².

items.solution: Applying A repeatedly leverages linearity A(λv) = λ(Av) = λ(λv) = λ²v.
hints: Always state the initial hypothesis first.
What algebraic operation introduces A² on the left hand side?
Group matrix multiplication using associativity: A(Av) = A²v.
Use the fact that scalars commute with matrices: A(λv) = λ(Av).
The correct sequence is step-1 -> step-2 -> step-3 -> step-4 -> step-5.

items.prompt: Explain why an eigenvector must correspond to a non-trivial nullspace of (A - λI), and why that forces det(A - λI) = 0.

rubricCriteria: Mentions that (A - λI)v = 0 is a rearrangement of Av = λv
Notes that eigenvectors must be non-zero (v ≠ 0) by definition
Explains that a non-zero vector in the nullspace implies the matrix is singular / non-invertible
Connects singularity of a matrix to det = 0 (collapsing of geometric volume)

items.solution: Av = λv rearranges to (A - λI)v = 0. Since v ≠ 0, (A - λI) sends a non-zero vector to zero, meaning its kernel/nullspace is non-trivial. A linear map with a non-trivial kernel is non-invertible and collapses at least one dimension, which means its signed volume scaling factor—the determinant—must be exactly zero.
